name: Bag wig

card.summary: An 18th-century men's wig whose tail was enclosed in a black silk bag, giving the wearer a neat, formal silhouette and a fuller head of hair.
card.aka: Bagwig, wig bag, perruque a la regence
card.note: Historical style; modern use is mainly costume and reenactment.

quick.overview:
A bag wig is a men's wig of the 18th century in which the long hair at the back was gathered into a queue and enclosed in a pouch of black silk or taffeta, tied with a drawstring and a bow. It gave a smooth, tidy outline and a fuller head of hair than the wearer's own.

Originally the bag protected the coat from the greased, powdered tail of the wig, and later it became purely ornamental. Museum collections hold surviving bags from the 1790s and 1800s.
quick.how: The wig was worn over the head, the back hair tied into a queue and slipped into the bag, which was secured with a drawstring hidden beneath a bow. Powder and grease were used to style the hair.
quick.risks: No health risks are documented in the sources; historical wigs were powdered and greased, which marked clothing, hence the bag.

lead: A bag wig (or bagwig) is an 18th-century men's wig whose queue, the tail of hair at the back, was enclosed in a black silk bag [2]. As a way of changing appearance it gave a formal, fuller hair outline regardless of the wearer's own hair.

The Victoria and Albert Museum records that such bags were originally used to hold the greased, powdered tail of a man's wig so it would not soil his coat, and later became purely ornamental [1]. A brief history of English wigs places queued wigs, either tied with a bow or in a black silk bag, among the shorter styles that appeared in the 1720s and 1730s [2].

angle.text: The wig provides the look of full, styled hair for the wearer, and the bag finishes the back with a neat, formal line. It is a historical style now mostly seen in costume and period reenactment.

infobox: Black silk taffeta or satin, canvas-lined [1]

paras: The back of the wig was gathered into a tail, or queue, and placed in a black silk bag [2]. A surviving British bag at the V&A dated 1790 to 1810 is black silk taffeta lined with canvas, rectangular and pleated at the top, about 34 cm long, with a bow-shaped silk trim [1].

Bobbed and queued wigs spread in the 1720s and 1730s, some worn tied with a bow (tie wig) and others in a silk bag [2]. The bag's function shifted from practical protection to decoration over the century [1].

timeline.event: Shorter bobbed and queued wigs, some bagged, come into fashion [2].
